Before you start

Students learn that most colleges admit most applicants, that where you go matters less than what you do there for most people, and they sort what's in their control. Bring index cards, and never ask where anyone applied, got in, or got deferred.

Every student in the room

On the Eli card, say plainly that staying close to home, community college, a gap year and the trades are real plans, and that families talk about money very differently.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students see that the selective schools they hear most about are a narrow slice of colleges, learn what the research says about whether prestige pays off, sort what they can and can't control, and pick one worry to stop feeding. Nobody shares where they're applying or what they got.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per student
  • A marker for the board
  • The student page link (last slide) to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minWhat everyone tells you (popcorn)
  2. 4 minThe whole picture: guess how many take under 1 in 10
  3. 4 minDoes the name pay off? Turn and talk, share out
  4. 6 minThree moments: Ava, Eli, Mia
  5. 3 minMore than one path; yours, not yours (private card)

Short on time (10-minute version)

The whole picture (3), does the name pay off (3), yours, not yours (4). Skip the scenarios or hand them out for later.

Before you teach
Results are private.

Some students got in early, some were deferred or denied, some haven't applied anywhere, and some aren't going to college next year. Never ask for a show of hands about outcomes. Keep every example invented.

Don't play admissions officer.

If a student asks about their own list or chances, point them to their college counselor. Your job here is the stress and the perspective, not the strategy.

Hold both truths.

The research says prestige matters less than most people think for most students, and it also finds real advantages at the very top, especially for students whose families lack those networks. Say both. Students trust a lesson that admits the complicated part.

Money is a quiet weight.

For some students, the whole process is about what their family can afford, and nobody has said the number out loud. Name money as part of fit without asking anyone about theirs.

Watch for the student who's sinking.

"My life is over because of one decision" is more than normal senior stress. If a student's sleep, eating or mood has been off for weeks, follow up one on one that day.

Seniors can be cynical.

Some will roll their eyes at "it doesn't matter where you go." Don't argue. Show them the Dale and Krueger finding and let them pick at it.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

First in the family.

Students who'd be first to go to college often carry extra pressure and less inside information. Name first-generation programs and fee waivers as normal tools, not charity.

Money looks different from seat to seat.

Net price, aid forms and loans mean very different things to different families. Talk about price as part of fit for everyone, and never use a student's family as an example.

Paths beyond the four-year campus.

Community college, a gap year, the military, trades and apprenticeships are real plans. Treat them as choices, with the same respect as any acceptance.

Family expectations vary.

In some families, staying close to home or contributing to the household is a value, not a failure to launch. In others, going far is the expectation. Present both as reasonable.

Who gets the advantage.

The research finds selective colleges help Black and Hispanic students and students whose parents have less formal education more than others. Present it as a fact about networks and access, never as a comment on any student's ability.

Learning differences and disability.

Students with learning plans, chronic illness or disabilities may also be weighing support services, distance from their doctors and testing accommodations. Mention that the right support is part of academic fit.

What the research says

Of 1,364 four-year colleges in a 2019 Pew analysis of federal data, more than half admitted at least two-thirds of applicants, and only 17 admitted fewer than 10%.

DeSilver, Pew Research Center, 2019

Comparing students who got into similar colleges but chose differently, the average earnings boost from attending the more selective school mostly disappeared once researchers accounted for where students applied and were admitted.

Dale and Krueger, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2002; Journal of Human Resources, 2014

The same research found a real benefit for Black and Hispanic students and for students whose parents had less formal education.

Dale and Krueger, 2002 and 2014

Attending an Ivy-Plus college instead of a selective public flagship raised the chances of reaching the top 1% of earners and of working at elite firms. Effects on average earnings were much smaller.

Chetty, Deming and Friedman, NBER working paper, 2023

In a survey of about 30,000 graduates, the type of college mattered little for later well-being and work engagement. Graduates who had a professor who cared about them, made them excited to learn and encouraged their goals had more than double the odds of thriving.

Gallup and Purdue University, 2014

Students at high-achieving schools show higher rates of anxiety, depression and substance use than many people expect, tied partly to constant pressure to excel. Close, accepting relationships with adults and friends who value them apart from achievement are protective.

Luthar, Kumar and Zillmer, American Psychologist, 2020
